claim_text: FCC 26-50 (adopted 22 Jul 2026, effective 13 Oct 2026) denies new equipment authorisations to devices containing a logic-bearing hardware component produced by a producer-based Covered List entity. It applies to new authorisations only; pending applications are exempt unless amended; software and firmware are excluded for now.
The component rule does not currently reach InnoLight or Eoptolink optics: neither company is a producer-based Covered List entity.
counter_evidence: Our reading of the rule's scope; no source names the two companies in this context.

claim_text: The FCC is reported to be drafting a ban on imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers. No draft text or threat determination has been published, and the FCC could modify or shelve it.
counter_evidence: Reported by four unnamed sources (Reuters); no official text.

claim_text: A transceiver rule is reported to phase in from the 3.2T generation (ramping around 2028–29), leaving current 800G and 1.6T outside the initial focus.
counter_evidence: Cignal AI (PR-012) argues revisions of 800G and 1.6T 'would certainly be considered new'; Fusion Worldwide (PR-016, Sept) rated 1.6T as high exposure. All reporting traces to Morgan Stanley notes; no official text.

claim_text: A possible exemption would allow Chinese-made transceivers if at least 65% of bill-of-materials value comes from US companies.
counter_evidence: Single reported chain (Economic Daily News citing Morgan Stanley, via TrendForce); PR-013 states it without a source. No official text; the definition of 'US company' is undecided.

claim_text: Chinese-assembled modules use US digital signal processors (Broadcom, Marvell) and US or Japanese lasers (Lumentum, Coherent, Mitsubishi Electric).

Whether a rule follows the company (entity) or the place of manufacture (origin) is unsettled. Under an origin rule, Thailand lines built by InnoLight and Eoptolink for North American demand may fall outside it. Industry is also unsure whether components and subsidiaries are covered.

S.5548 (introduced 24 Sep 2026) would bar federal procurement of optical transceivers from InnoLight, Eoptolink, their subsidiaries and affiliates, and later-designated entities. Prohibitions take effect five years after enactment; the FAR Council must update rules within three years. Status: introduced, referred to HSGAC.

Zhongji Innolight was added to the Department of War 1260H list on 8 Jun 2026 (188 entities). The Section 805 entity contracting ban applies from 30 Jun 2026; the product ban from 30 Jun 2027 excludes components inside end items.

Foreign-produced power inverters were added to the Covered List on 28 Jul 2026, narrowed on 20 Aug 2026 to utility-interactive inverters meeting UL 1741 with remote communications. Previously authorised models are unaffected; Conditional Approval applications are due by 1 Jan 2028.
counter_evidence: Davis Wright Tremaine: ordinary data-centre UPS and rectifiers are 'less likely to be covered'.

claim_text: Foreign-produced consumer-grade routers were added to the Covered List on 23 Mar 2026. Scope is residential, customer-installed devices, generally not data-centre networking. Conditional Approvals listed as of 4 Jun 2026 end between 1 Oct and 5 Dec 2027.
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, on FCC 26-50: “First, we take action to finally and fully close the component part loophole.”

Sponsors of S.5548 (Sens. McCormick, Gallego, Cornyn, Fetterman): “Because advanced transceivers can contain reprogrammable firmware, their use in national security networks can create potential supply-chain and security risks.” Sen. Gallego: “Our reliance on China to produce these transceivers creates a serious national security vulnerability.”
counter_evidence: Two of the four sponsor statements also make a domestic-manufacturing argument (PR-026).

claim_text: Microsoft and other technology companies are reported to have urged the administration to drop the plan, citing supply-chain disruption (meetings with OSTP and NSC in September).
counter_evidence: Reported (Reuters, via TrendForce and SDxCentral); no statement from Microsoft.

claim_text: Analysts and networking vendors point to capacity, cost and timing: non-Chinese makers lack capacity to absorb the volume within 12–24 months, standing up new lines would take two to three years, and the system is interdependent (US DSPs and lasers inside Chinese-assembled modules).

No confirmed data-access or security incident involving InnoLight or Eoptolink transceivers has been publicly reported (“No malicious transceiver firmware has been publicly documented”). Modules do carry microcontrollers and firmware.
counter_evidence: ChinaTalk adds: “The absence of a public example isn't disproof.” Beacon Global Strategies (quoted by Reuters): “Transceivers definitely pose a risk.” Cignal AI: “There is no bona fide security risk.”
notes: Risk-assessment caveat (brief's 'optics are hardware' line dropped: modules run firmware)

claim_text: InnoLight, on its 1260H designation: the designation “does not accord with objective facts”; it is “neither a Chinese military company nor a military-civil fusion enterprise”.

China's embassy in Washington, on the reported FCC plan: “China will take all necessary measures in response to any action that causes material harm to its interests.” Eoptolink said it was watching the impact and that the report had no authoritative source yet.
counter_evidence: No public response to S.5548 by the companies or the Chinese government was found at build date.

claim_text: The reported design (new models only, from 3.2T, with a BOM exemption) limits near-term supply effects. This is an observation about the design, not a finding of intent.
counter_evidence: Administrative feasibility; the FCC's stated legal-basis reasoning for the narrower component definition (limited to components “within our statutory authority to regulate under the Communications Act”, PR-001); giving allied capacity time to build (the S.5548 five-year transition, PR-021).
notes: Design-choice reading. Intent rule: no claim beyond 'consistent with a deliberate choice'
